The selling curriculum — seven modules

1
Know the product — Tab 01

Keyman is corporate liquidity: company proposes, pays, and receives. Learn the one-line pitch until you can say it cold: "Your balance sheet says the business is strong. Your revenue history says it is strong because of one or two people. This programme converts that concentration risk into a funded plan."

2
Hunt the right prospect — Tab 02

Profitable limited company, owner-managed, profit swings that track one person, bank debt, no succession plan. Score every business client you already have — your renewal book is full of keyman prospects. Drill: qualify three existing clients this week.

3
Open the first meeting

Never open with insurance. Open with their numbers: "I went through your last three years. Revenue moved from X to Y. Can I show you what that trajectory says about the business?" You are demonstrating the file understands them. The product enters the room last.

4
Run the valuation LIVE — Tab 03

Enter their financials in the meeting and hand them the attribution slider. When the client sets their own percentage, the sum assured becomes their number, not yours. Drill: load the worked example and practise narrating every band on the chart out loud.

5
Handle the pushback — Tab 05

You will hear "we have cash", "profits jump around", and "why this number" — rehearse all nine responses until the client can't surprise you. Drill: pair up; one plays the sceptical finance director for ten minutes.

6
Close and apply — Tab 08

The close is a process, not a moment: agree the lives and sums, lock the medical dates before forms circulate, then open the file in the Apply tab — collect the audited three-year financials and the Annual Return (shareholdings), attach them in the document slots, download the case pack, and the GLOC forms generate themselves.

7
After lodgement — the second sale

Every placed keyman file has a Phase 2: shareholder protection, buy-sell funding, the loan-account strategy. Diarise it. The relationship you just built is the pipeline.

The Playbook

Keyman insurance is a policy a company takes out on the life (and health) of the people its earnings actually depend on. The company proposes, pays and receives the claim. It is not a payroll benefit — it is corporate liquidity, delivered at the exact event that threatens the business.

Who it protects
The company
Proposer & beneficiary
Proceeds land on the company's balance sheet to replace profit, service debt and fund a replacement — not in a family member's hands.
What it covers
Life + CI
Death & critical illness
Critical illness acceleration matters: survival of the person can still mean interruption of the business for 12–24 months.
Who buys it
Owner-led firms
Profitable & concentrated
Businesses where revenue tracks one or two people: contractors, energy services, equipment rental, distribution, professional practices.
The one-line pitch. "Your balance sheet says the business is strong. Your revenue history says it is strong because of one or two people. This programme converts that concentration risk into a funded plan — for an annual cost that is a rounding error on your accounts."

Prospect signals — who to call first

  • Profitable limited company, owner-managed, 10+ years trading
  • Profit swings that track contract wins by the principal
  • Bank facilities, demand loans or overdrafts in place
  • Large shareholder loan accounts on the balance sheet
  • No shareholders' agreement or succession plan
  • Recent growth, new contracts, or fleet/plant reinvestment
  • Key people aged under ~60 — insurability is perishable

The four financial tests

Every defensible sum assured sits where these intersect. The Valuation Engine (Tab 03) computes all four live:

Salary multiple5–10× annual remuneration of the key person
Profit corridor5× the pre-tax profit attributable to the key person
Gross profit test2× attributable gross profit — the floor
Debt envelopeBank facilities + shareholder loans fully enveloped

Sanity cap: the aggregate should stay well below the company's indicative value — typically under 20% of book equity.

Choosing the vehicle — term, whole life, or both

Term insures the event. Whole life insures the person leaving by any door. Only three of the nine key-person risks pay a claim; the rest need a vehicle that still has value when nobody dies.

LayerWhat it doesSized on
Whole life — the corePermanent. Builds cash value the company owns. Still in force at 70 to fund the Phase 2 shareholder buy-out. Leaves an asset if the key person emigrates, burns out or retires.What the company can sustain permanently
Term — the top-upCheap cover for a big number. Matched to the recovery window or the bank facility, and it expires when that exposure does.The gap to the full quantified sum
RidersCritical illness acceleration and total & permanent disability — two of the three insurable risks are not death.Maximum issuable
The clause almost nobody writes. Agree in the board resolution what happens to the policy if the key person leaves: surrender it, transfer it to them as an exit or retirement benefit, or re-designate it to their successor. That single line is what makes the vehicle answer emigration, burnout and departure — the risks no claim will ever cover.
Say these before the client finds them. Cash value builds slowly — treat it as a ten-year-plus asset, not year-three liquidity. Every dollar into cash value is a dollar not buying cover, so a whole-life-only structure can leave the company under-insured against the very exposure you quantified. And the policy is a company asset: it sits on the balance sheet and can affect share value in a buy-sell. Confirm the tax and accounting treatment with Guardian technical in writing before it goes in a client dossier.
Objection gold. Whole life reframes "we have cash, why insure?" — it is not an expense that may never pay, it is a funded reserve that pays at the worst moment and stays the company's asset if it doesn't. Reinsurers underwrite the sum assured, not the product — never tell a client the reinsurer required a particular vehicle.

When the obvious life is uninsurable — the pivot plays

Shareholders in their 70s are above viable new-business issue age. That is not the end of the case — it is a different case. Four structures this branch has placed or recommended:

Pivot 1

Company sinking fund — annual set-aside from profits toward the future buyout.

Pivot 2

Instalment buy-sell — 3–5 year payout of the deceased's stake, agreed now.

Pivot 3

Cross-option + cover on the successor — insure the next generation who must fund the purchase.

Pivot 4

Accelerated share transfer — move equity to the successor now, insure the tax and funding gap.

Always insure the successor generation for keyman even when the elders hold the shares — the operating risk usually sits with the people running the business day to day, and they are the insurable lives.

Process & Evidence

This case is won in two meetings if the sequence is respected. The discipline that matters most: medical dates locked before any form circulates. Draft figures in circulation create version-control risk at signing.

The six-step sequence

1
Open with the numbers — on screen, not on paper

Walk the client's own hero figures. Let them correct or confirm the picture. You are not selling yet; you are demonstrating that the file understands them.

2
Run the Valuation Engine live

Hand them the attribution slider. When the client sets their own percentage, the sum assured becomes their number, not yours. Note what they choose — it goes in the submission narrative.

3
Agree lives, names and the aggregate in the Coverage Builder

Confirm the key lives, capture full names and dates of birth, lock the per-life sums.

4
Lock the medical dates before any form circulates

Examiner appointments first, finalised forms second. One set of forms, one set of figures, one signing session.

5
Lodge with the evidence pack attached

A pre-answered file moves through financial underwriting in days, not weeks. Disclose hygiene items up front.

6
Diarise Phase 2 — shareholder protection

Once the share register and shareholder ages are confirmed: buy-sell funding, the shareholders' agreement, loan-account strategy. The second placement inside the same relationship.

Information required from the client

  • Full names, dates of birth and roles of each key life
  • Smoker status & brief medical history headlines
  • Three years of financial statements (audited where available)
  • Annual Return / share register — shareholdings and shareholder ages
  • Bank facility letters for all loans and overdrafts
  • Confirmation of audit status, or accountant's letter

Lodgement checklist

  • Valuation narrative with client-chosen attribution %
  • Sum assured inside the 5× profit corridor
  • Debt exposure enveloped and evidenced
  • Board resolution — company as proposer & beneficiary
  • Medical appointments completed
  • Hygiene items disclosed up front
